## Precision and Recall: Core Classification Metrics

### 1. Introduction

When evaluating a classification model, raw accuracy can often provide an incomplete picture, especially when one class is significantly rarer than the other [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Plain-English Interpretation]. **Precision** and **Recall** are two core classification metrics that address this by measuring different dimensions of a model's ability to correctly and completely identify the positive class [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Plain-English Interpretation]. Precision answers the question, "Are my Positive predictions correct?", while Recall asks, "Did I find ALL the real Positives?" [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Plain-English Interpretation]. Both metrics range from 0 to 1 [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Plain-English Interpretation].

### 2. Key Concepts

#### Precision
**Precision** measures how trustworthy a model's positive predictions are, indicating how often the model is actually right when it predicts a positive case [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: 1. Precision]. It is known as the metric of **exactness**, where a high-precision model rarely raises false alarms [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: 1. Precision].

*   **Plain-English Interpretation:** Imagine a detective filing arrest warrants; precision is the fraction of issued warrants that result in a valid conviction [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Plain-English Interpretation]. A low-precision detective arrests too many innocent people [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Plain-English Interpretation].
*   **Real-World Analogies:**
    *   **Spam Filter:** Precision is the fraction of emails flagged as spam that are genuinely spam [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Real-World Analogies]. Low precision means legitimate emails are blocked, leading to user distrust [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Real-World Analogies].
    *   **Search Engine:** Precision@10 is the fraction of the top 10 results that are truly relevant [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Real-World Analogies]. Low precision forces users to scroll past irrelevant links [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Real-World Analogies].
*   **What Lowers Precision:**
    *   **Low decision threshold:** The model predicts Positive too liberally, leading to more False Positives (FP) [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 2, Section: What Lowers Precision?].
    *   **Noisy/irrelevant features:** The model confuses negatives for positives [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 2, Section: What Lowers Precision?].
    *   **Severe class imbalance:** A large negative pool creates more opportunities for FP [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 2, Section: What Lowers Precision?].
    *   **Overly broad boundary:** The positive region captures many true negatives [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 2, Section: What Lowers Precision?].
*   **How to Improve Precision:** Raise the decision threshold, add stronger/cleaner features, apply higher misclassification cost on FP during training, or use precision-oriented resampling strategies [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 2, Section: What Lowers Precision?].

#### Recall
**Recall** measures how completely the model finds all real positive cases, indicating how many actual positives in the data the model caught [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: 2. Recall]. It is known as the metric of **completeness**, where a high-recall model misses very few real cases [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: 2. Recall]. Recall is also referred to as **Sensitivity** or **True Positive Rate (TPR)** [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: 2. Recall].

*   **Plain-English Interpretation:** Continuing the detective analogy, recall is the fraction of all real criminals that the detective actually caught [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: Plain-English Interpretation]. Low recall means guilty parties walk free [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: Plain-English Interpretation].
*   **Real-World Analogies:**
    *   **Cancer Screening:** Recall is the fraction of all cancer patients correctly identified [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: Real-World Analogies]. Low recall means sick patients are sent home without treatment [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: Real-World Analogies].
    *   **Fraud Detection:** Recall is the fraction of all fraudulent transactions that get flagged [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: Real-World Analogies]. Low recall means fraudsters slip through undetected [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: Real-World Analogies].
*   **What Lowers Recall:**
    *   **High decision threshold:** The model predicts Positive too conservatively, leading to more False Negatives (FN) [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 4, Section: What Lowers Recall?].
    *   **Positive class under-represented:** The model has rarely seen enough positive examples to learn from [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 4, Section: What Lowers Recall?].
    *   **Severe class imbalance:** The minority class is "drowned out" during training [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 4, Section: What Lowers Recall?].
    *   **Overly conservative boundary:** The model prefers "safe" negative predictions [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 4, Section: What Lowers Recall?].
*   **How to Improve Recall:** Lower the decision threshold, oversample positives (e.g., SMOTE), assign higher misclassification cost to FN, or use ensemble methods that boost sensitivity on rare classes [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 5, Section: How to improve Recall].

#### The Precision–Recall Trade-off
Precision and Recall are in tension, meaning that adjusting the classification threshold typically moves one metric up while pulling the other down [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 5, Section: 3. The Precision–Recall Trade-off]. This dynamic is crucial in applied machine learning [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 5, Section: 3. The Precision–Recall Trade-off].

*   **How the Threshold Drives Both Metrics:**
    *   **Very High Threshold (≥0.95):** Predicts Positive only when near-certain, leading to high Precision and low Recall [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 5, Section: How the Threshold Drives Both Metrics].
    *   **Very Low Threshold (≤0.10):** Predicts Positive very liberally, leading to low Precision and high Recall [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 5, Section: How the Threshold Drives Both Metrics].
*   **Why the Trade-off Exists:** Lowering the threshold makes the model predict Positive more often, catching more real positives (Recall increases) but also flagging more negatives as positive (Precision decreases) [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 5, Section: Why the Trade-off Exists]. Conversely, raising the threshold makes the model predict Positive only when very confident, resulting in fewer false alarms (Precision increases) but missing some real positives (Recall decreases) [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 5, Section: Why the Trade-off Exists]. It is impossible to simultaneously maximize both metrics with a single threshold [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 5, Section: Why the Trade-off Exists].
*   **Threshold Selection in Practice:** The choice of threshold depends on the specific goal [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 5, Section: Threshold Selection in Practice]. For example, to maximize F1 Score, one might find a threshold where Precision is approximately equal to Recall on a validation set [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 5, Section: Threshold Selection in Practice]. To minimize false alarms, the threshold can be raised until Precision meets a business Service Level Agreement (SLA) [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 5, Section: Threshold Selection in Practice]. To maximize coverage, the threshold can be lowered until Recall meets a clinical requirement [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 5, Section: Threshold Selection in Practice].

#### The Precision–Recall Curve & AUPRC
Instead of evaluating at a single threshold, the **Precision–Recall Curve** plots Precision (y-axis) against Recall (x-axis) across every possible threshold, providing a full picture of the trade-off space [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 6, Section: 4. The Precision–Recall Curve & AUPRC].

![Infographic - Precision-Recall Curve Example](http://localhost:8001/static/generated_content/ml/precision_and_recall/notes/v1_infographic.png)

*   **Area Under the PR Curve (AUPRC):** The AUPRC summarizes the entire curve as a single number between 0 and 1, where a higher value is better [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 7, Section: Area Under the PR Curve (AUPRC)]. It is particularly valuable for imbalanced datasets because it focuses solely on the positive class and is not inflated by a large number of true negatives, unlike AUC-ROC [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 7, Section: Area Under the PR Curve (AUPRC)]. As a rule of thumb, a random classifier on a dataset with 10% positive class has an AUPRC of approximately 0.10; a useful model should significantly exceed the positive class prevalence [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 7, Section: Area Under the PR Curve (AUPRC)]. AUPRC should be used whenever classes are highly imbalanced [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 7, Section: Area Under the PR Curve (AUPRC)].

#### Numeric Model Comparison
Different models can exhibit varying performance across Precision and Recall [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 7, Section: 5. Numeric Model Comparison]. For example, an "Aggressive" model might have high recall but low precision, while a "Conservative" model might have high precision but low recall [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 7, Section: 5. Numeric Model Comparison]. A "Balanced" model aims for solid performance on both, and a "Near-perfect" model achieves strong results in both metrics [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 7, Section: 5. Numeric Model Comparison].

#### When to Prioritise Each Metric
The decision to prioritize Precision or Recall depends on the specific costs associated with different types of errors [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 8, Section: 6. When to Prioritise Each Metric].

*   **Prioritise PRECISION When:**
    *   False alarms are costly (e.g., spam blocking real mail) [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 8, Section: 6. When to Prioritise Each Metric].
    *   User trust depends on accuracy (e.g., recommendation engines) [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 8, Section: 6. When to Prioritise Each Metric].
    *   Resources to act on alerts are scarce (e.g., security analyst capacity) [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 8, Section: 6. When to Prioritise Each Metric].
    *   A wrong positive has a high financial cost (e.g., expensive lab test ordered) [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 8, Section: 6. When to Prioritise Each Metric].
*   **Prioritise RECALL When:**
    *   Missing a positive is dangerous (e.g., cancer diagnosis) [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 8, Section: 6. When to Prioritise Each Metric].
    *   Coverage is the primary goal (e.g., content moderation) [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 8, Section: 6. When to Prioritise Each Metric].
    *   All positives MUST be found (e.g., regulatory compliance) [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 8, Section: 6. When to Prioritise Each Metric].
    *   A wrong negative has a high human cost (e.g., disease untreated) [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 8, Section: 6. When to Prioritise Each Metric].

### 3. Formulae

*   **Precision = TP / (TP + FP)** [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Formula]
    *   **TP** (True Positives) are correct positive predictions [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Formula].
    *   **FP** (False Positives) are incorrect positive predictions [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Formula].
    *   The denominator (TP + FP) represents every instance the model predicted as positive [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Formula].
*   **Recall = TP / (TP + FN)** [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: Formula]
    *   **FN** (False Negatives) are actual positives the model failed to detect [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: Formula].
    *   The denominator (TP + FN) represents the total number of real positives in the dataset [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: Formula].

### 4. Examples

#### Worked Numeric Example for Precision
A medical imaging AI scans 500 X-rays and flags 80 as showing pneumonia [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 2, Section: Worked Numeric Example]. After expert review, 64 of those 80 are confirmed cases, and 16 are not [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 2, Section: Worked Numeric Example].
*   True Positives (TP) = 64 [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 2, Section: Worked Numeric Example]
*   False Positives (FP) = 16 [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 2, Section: Worked Numeric Example]
*   Precision = 64 / (64 + 16) = 64 / 80 = **0.80** [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 2, Section: Worked Numeric Example]
This means the model is correct 80% of the time it raises an alert, with one in five alerts being a false alarm [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 2, Section: Worked Numeric Example].

#### Worked Numeric Example for Recall
There are 100 actual pneumonia cases across the 500 X-rays [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: Worked Numeric Example]. The AI found 64 of them and missed 36 [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: Worked Numeric Example].
*   True Positives (TP) = 64 [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: Worked Numeric Example]
*   False Negatives (FN) = 36 [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: Worked Numeric Example]
*   Recall = 64 / (64 + 36) = 64 / 100 = **0.64** [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 3, Section: Worked Numeric Example]
The model detected only 64% of real pneumonia cases, meaning 36 patients were incorrectly cleared [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 1, Section: Worked Numeric Example].

#### Python Code Example
The `sklearn.metrics` module provides functions for calculating precision and recall [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 8, Section: Python Code].

```python
from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score, precision_recall_curve
y_true = [0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0]
y_pred = [0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0]
y_prob = [.1, .9, .4, .2, .8, .7, .6, .3, .85, .15]
# Point metrics at default 0.5 threshold
p = precision_score(y_true, y_pred)
r = recall_score(y_true, y_pred)
print(f"Precision: {p:.3f} | Recall: {r:.3f}")
# Full PR Curve (threshold-independent)
prec, rec, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(y_true, y_prob)
```
[Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 8, Section: Python Code]

### 5. Summary

*   **Precision** is calculated as TP / (TP+FP) and measures exactness, answering "when I say positive, am I right?" [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 9, Section: Key Takeaways].
*   **Recall** is calculated as TP / (TP+FN) and measures completeness, answering "did I find all the real positives?" [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 9, Section: Key Takeaways].
*   There is a **trade-off** between Precision and Recall: raising the decision threshold increases Precision and decreases Recall, while lowering it decreases Precision and increases Recall [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 9, Section: Key Takeaways].
*   No single threshold can maximize both metrics simultaneously; the choice depends on the specific costs of errors in the application [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 9, Section: Key Takeaways].
*   The **Precision–Recall Curve** and **AUPRC** are useful for threshold-independent model comparison, especially with imbalanced datasets [Source: precision_recall.pdf, Page 9, Section: Key Takeaways].
